inputs.original_text: Father Bernard Domini, superior of the Missionary Family of Notre-Dame, has been convicted under France’s new law on “psychological subjection.” Protecting people from coercion matters, but a law with such a broad-sounding target also raises serious civil-liberties concerns: the state must not be allowed to punish belief or association without clear, rigorous safeguards. The alarm from religious communities and civil-liberties advocates should be taken seriously. A just response to harm must protect vulnerable people without handing institutions vague powers over private life.
inputs.modified_text: Father Bernard Domini, superior of the Missionary Family of Notre-Dame, has been convicted under France’s new law on “psychological subjection.” The concern should not be only whether religious communities face state scrutiny, but whether people vulnerable to coercion have meaningful protection from powerful institutions. At the same time, broad laws need clear safeguards: justice means taking harm seriously without giving the state vague authority over belief or association. Both protection and civil liberties require accountability, not deference to institutional power.
